text: You've installed Terraform, run its core workflow, and seen how resources, data sources, and state fit together. This last Chapter 1 lesson covers the three HCL building blocks almost every real configuration leans on: variable, output, and locals.

A variable block declares a named input, with an optional type, default, and description. location has a default of eastus, so it's optional to supply. environment has no default, so Terraform will prompt for it, or refuse to run non-interactively, unless you pass one — typically with -var equals environment equals dev on the command line, or a .tfvars file. You reference either one elsewhere as var.location and var.environment, which is what lets the same configuration deploy dev today and prod tomorrow without touching the .tf files.

An output block exposes a value once apply finishes. value equals azurerm_resource_group.rg.id prints that resource group's real ID to the console after apply, and terraform output resource_group_id retrieves it on demand afterward. This is also how one Terraform configuration feeds values into another — a networking config can output a VNet ID that an application config later reads, instead of hard-coding it or redeclaring the same resource twice.

A locals block defines named values computed from other expressions, meant to be reused inside this configuration — not supplied from outside like a variable, not exposed outside like an output. resource_group_name built from var.environment, and a common_tags map, are both typical locals: compute a naming convention or a tag map once, in one place, instead of retyping the same expression on every resource.

Put all three together and you get the shape nearly every real Terraform configuration takes: environment comes in as a variable, locals derives a naming convention and tag map from it once, the resource block consumes both for its name and tags, and output exposes the resource group's ID once it's real.

That's Chapter 1 — installing Terraform and the provider model, the init-plan-apply workflow, resources versus data sources against the state file, and now variables, outputs, and locals. Chapter 2 opens by putting all of it to work for real: provisioning an actual Azure resource group and VNet with Terraform.
